extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research funders, policy-makers and evaluators interested in grant peer review, equity, and administrative burden
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidence-based criteria for identifying, measuring, and reducing bias and administrative burden in grant funding processes (peer review, scoring, and program design). Focuses on applicant- and reviewer-level factors, measurement approaches, and mitigation strategies used by international funders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Association between application outcome and gender (e.g., studies using multilevel regression over 1999–2009 found no statistically significant association; meta-analyses report both little and substantial effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite meta-analyses and field-specific studies; consider conflicting evidence (Mutz et al., 2012; Ceci & Williams, 2011; Bornmann et al., 2007) when assessing whether gender affects funding outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant race / racial bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that race affects funding outcomes (e.g., NIH 2011 finding: black applicants were ten percentage points less likely to obtain R01 funding after controlling for many external factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control extensively for confounds (education, training, prior awards, publications, employer characteristics); consider experiments (name-swapping) that assess reviewer-level effects and other stages of the funding process (Forscher et al., 2018).

rubrics_metrics.name: Career stage (career age vs competencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Career stage as a potential source of bias — e.g., ageing researcher population may crowd-out early-career researchers; career age often measured as years since highest doctoral degree but has limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about how 'career stage' is defined (career age, competences, or frameworks like the European Framework for Research Careers) because measurement choice affects detection of bias and policy responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research field and interdisciplinarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias between research fields and against interdisciplinary research; interdisciplinary proposals may be less likely to be funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative metrics (e.g., interdisciplinary distance (IDD) metric) to capture representation and distance between fields (Bromham et al., 2016) when evaluating funding probabilities for interdisciplinary proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional attributes (e.g., small vs large institutions) may affect funding success and quantity (NSERC study found lower success and quantity for small institutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate effects of institutional merit vs research environment; use statistical analysis and forecasting models to detect and adjust for institutional disparities (Murray et al., 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer characteristics (expertise, intellectual closeness, nationality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer attributes influence evaluations: intellectually closer reviewers may be slightly more likely to fund; reviewers with more self-rated expertise sometimes score harsher; nationality of reviewers affects ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reviewer–applicant intellectual distance (e.g., citation-based closeness), collect reviewer self-assessed expertise and nationality, and account for these in analyses of scoring patterns (Li, 2017; Gallo et al., 2016; Marsh et al., 2008).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability (agreement among reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of agreement among raters is central to peer review; historical studies show 24–35% disagreement, while some trials report higher agreement (e.g., 83% in an NHMRC Early Career Fellowship duplicated review study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify inter-rater reliability for panels/competitions and investigate how scoring/assessment criteria or application types (e.g., early career) affect agreement levels (Clarke et al., 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted grant streams for disadvantaged groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeted funding streams (e.g., NIH K02, MRC New Investigator, ERC Starting Grants) designed to support applicants disadvantaged by biases or program structure, such as early career researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether targeted streams correct observed disparities and monitor potential unintended consequences; include appropriate eligibility and evaluation criteria focused on intended beneficiaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training on unconscious bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Training modules on unconscious biases can reduce bias and increase inter-rater reliability (CIHR introduced training and subsequent cycles showed equal success rates for men and women; NIH online training increased reviewer correlation from 0.61 to 0.89).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement and evaluate bias-awareness training for reviewers; measure pre/post changes in success rates and inter-rater reliability to assess effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding / anonymisation of applicant identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymising applicant identity from reviewers (double-blind review) can increase representation of under-represented groups (e.g., Behavioural Ecology saw a 33% increase in female authors' representation); NSF 'The Big Pitch' tested anonymised brief proposals with mixed correlation to full outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider blinded review trials for funding competitions, monitor effects on representation and overall selection quality, and be aware that blinding may affect only some stages of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative burden on applicants, reviewers, funders, and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant application process is time-consuming and costly for applicants, reviewers, funding agencies, and institutions; increasing application volume and shrinking funds exacerbate the burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure burden across stakeholders and consider reforms that lower time/cost (simplified forms, shorter proposals, fewer reviewers) while preserving selection quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring burden via surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys are frequently used to assess time spent preparing applications and reviewing, and distribution of time among activities (Herbert et al., 2013/2014; Kulage et al., 2015; Schroter et al., 2010).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design representative surveys asking about average time per activity, include respondent characteristics, and use results to estimate aggregate time costs and hotspots for streamlining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational studies of proposal preparation and progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Use observational studies to measure time spent preparing proposals, the use of simplified scoring (reject/revise/invite), and progression from submission to outcome (Barnett et al., 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect detailed time-use data across proposal stages and pilot simplified review/decision models to observe impacts on time and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating monetary cost of proposal preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate application costs by tracking time spent and combining with salaries, fringe rates, and facilities & administrative (F&A) cost recovery rates for personnel (Kulage et al., 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time-use data plus institution-specific salary and overhead figures to produce monetary estimates of application burden for policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum number of reviewers required for reliable scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing the minimum number of reviewers/panellists needed to obtain reliable and consistent funding decisions to reduce reviewer burden (studies used agreement analysis and bootstrapping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical agreement analyses or bootstrap replicates of scores to identify the trade-off between number of reviewers and decision reliability (Liaw et al., 2017; Snell, 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplified scoring systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simplified scoring of grant proposals (e.g., reject, revise, or invite to interview) as an approach to reduce burden and speed decision-making (observed in health services funding observational studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot simplified scoring schemes, evaluate effects on workload and selection accuracy, and compare progression rates and downstream outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of brief anonymised proposals alongside full proposals ('two-stage' anonymised briefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials such as NSF's 'The Big Pitch' require an anonymised two-page proposal alongside a full conventional proposal to test blinded selection and reduce reviewer load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare outcomes between brief anonymised submissions and full proposals to evaluate correlation and whether a brief can screen effectively while reducing reviewer time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative detection/forecasting of bias using statistical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysing large datasets of proposal review scores using logistic regression and forecasting models to detect patterns of funding success and institutional differences (e.g., Murray et al., 2016 developed forecasting model parameterised on 13,526 proposal review scores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ regression/forecasting models that control for applicant and institutional covariates to identify systematic disparities and to inform policy interventions.
